changes.after: Read only as much text as the available space can hold. Always check whether reading worked.

before: A char array reserves several character-sized positions. char name[6]; reserves six positions; C text uses a zero character to mark where the string ends.
fgets(name, sizeof name, stdin) reads from standard input into that array. sizeof name supplies its size, 6. fgets stores at most five input characters and a terminating zero character.
fgets returns a pointer to the array on success, or a null pointer on failure/end of input before any characters. A pointer identifies a location; checking != NULL asks whether reading succeeded.
Only print the buffer after a successful read. printf("%s", name); displays the stored string. %s must receive valid terminated text, not an integer.
If a newline fits, fgets keeps it. A longer line does not all fit: remaining input stays unread. This first exercise handles one short line; it is not a complete long-line validation system.
after: An array stores items next to each other. `char name[6]` makes room for six character-sized units. A C string is text ending with a zero character, written `\0`. That ending needs one space too.
`fgets` reads text into this array. `sizeof name` gives the space available: 6. For the plain letters in this lesson, fgets stores at most five input characters, then the ending zero.

`stdin` means the program's standard input, usually the keyboard. If fgets reads something, it returns a pointer: a value that refers to its location. `NULL` means no location. The `!= NULL` check asks whether the read worked.
Print name only when the read succeeds. `%s` tells printf to print a string up to its ending zero. If no text was read, the program prints No line received instead.
If a newline fits, fgets keeps it. If the line is too long, the remaining input waits to be read later. This example reads once; it does not collect or reject a whole long line.

before.question: Input is ABCDEFG followed by a newline. What is stored by this single fgets call?
choices: All seven letters: arrays grow automatically.
ABCDE plus a terminating zero character; the rest remains unread.
Nothing: fgets refuses every longer line.
before.explanation: Six positions allow five input characters and the terminator. The unread remainder is not automatically discarded.

after.question: The input is ABCDEFG followed by Enter. What does this one fgets call store?
choices: All seven letters, because the array grows.
ABCDE and the ending zero; the rest waits unread.
Nothing, because the line is too long.
after.explanation: The six spaces hold five letters and the ending zero. F, G, and the newline remain unread.
